items.question: How do you distinguish the synthetic data used in autonomous driving and embodied intelligence from other forms of synthetic data?
items.object: Synthetic data in autonomous driving and embodied intelligence
items.answer: Synthetic data is data generated through automated, programmatic methods. Such methods can take different forms: data may be generated through simulation, through algorithms, or through a combination of the two. At Photon Intelligence, we use more of a hybrid approach to synthetic data. Synthetic data also comes in different forms. The earliest examples in CV—computer vision—were perhaps 2D annotated data. In finance, data expanded through statistical methods is also called synthetic data. Today, for autonomous driving or embodied intelligence, synthetic data more often means 3D data with robot trajectories, perhaps even human-in-the-loop data. That is likely the synthetic data we will focus on today.

items.question: How do you assess Cruise’s Matrix project, which recreated San Francisco in a game engine for self-driving simulation?
items.object: Cruise’s Matrix simulation system
items.answer: In the earliest days, simulation recruited a group of game developers—engineers using Unreal Engine and similar tools. They built something called Matrix, named after The Matrix. items.question: Why do you think Cruise’s original simulation approach failed to bridge the gap between simulation and reality?
items.object: Cruise’s original approach to simulation and the Sim2Real gap
items.answer: The gap was the Sim2Real issue: there was a very large gap between simulation and reality. At the same time, those engineers had no expectation of solving it. They came from games; their goal was to make something that looked dazzling and exciting, not to solve the problem of producing real data required by robots or machine learning. Most importantly, nobody was trying to solve those gaps. They were trying to solve whether a car looked real visually, or whether a tree looked real visually, rather than whether feeding the generated data to a model would effectively improve it.

items.question: How did you approach making Cruise’s synthetic data useful for training perception models?
items.object: Evaluating and improving synthetic data for Cruise’s perception models
items.answer: I first defined the requirements for simulation and synthetic data from a machine-learning perspective: the data had to be supported by a pipeline such that adding data to feed the model would improve the model’s performance. That is the real way to validate the effectiveness of synthetic data. The first thing I did was not improve synthetic data or simulation, but build an evaluation system. I think that was a crucial point. Second, by building that evaluation system, I found major problems—a major gap—in simulation and synthetic data. They were trying to solve whether a car looked real visually, or whether a tree looked real visually, rather than whether feeding the generated data to a model would effectively improve it. I used that reverse direction to help define what needed improving: not only visual realism, but also distributions, sensor models, the realism of noise, and so forth. At those levels, I proposed using AI to improve the data itself. This was 2018, when GANs were still a very early, very basic form of generative AI. They compared real and synthetic data, tried to minimize the gap between them, and transferred aspects of real-data style onto synthetic data. For example, the sky might be grayer or the sensor might have more noise. Those were relatively basic generative-AI techniques used to improve the data. With those methods, and because we had evaluation criteria, we increasingly understood the entire stack: the assets themselves, scenario distributions, sensor simulation, and the quality of the whole data-generation chain. That allowed us to keep improving it. I did not solve it in three months as I had with maps; it took about six months. But in six months we did build a synthetic-data solution that could effectively improve our perception models.

items.question: How do you think a synthetic-data pipeline should be built to produce data that improves a model?
items.object: Synthetic-data pipelines for improving models
items.answer: At a high level, a data pipeline is an input, an output, and a pipeline in between. The input may include scenarios defined by people, scenarios observed in the real world, and variations based on them. For example, a hazardous situation encountered on the road, such as a bicycle ahead. Then you insert it. Starting from that base scenario, we can generalize it through statistical, manual, or AI methods, creating more scenarios and many assets. Assets may include bicycles, cars, the entire ground surface, surrounding trees, and so on. We generate a world from combinations of static assets and dynamic scenarios. On that basis, sensor simulation observes and outputs the data from the vehicle’s perspective. The pipeline may also include annotations. Automated annotation. At the time, annotations were still often 2D, computer-vision annotations—boxes around people, cars, and so on, plus semantic labels such as “this is a person” and “that is a car.” Later there increasingly came to be 3D and even 4D annotations, including semantic information. At the end of the pipeline is also a quality-inspection stage. We found this to be extremely critical: through automated and human-in-the-loop methods, it truly verifies the quality of the output data. It effectively ensures that our data can truly be used to improve the final model.

items.question: How do you think synthetic data should be evaluated for its value to a model?
items.object: Absolute evaluation and utility evaluation of synthetic data
items.answer: At the time, we conceived of two broad categories of criteria from first principles. The first was absolute evaluation: how real is it? This mainly meant benchmarking the output data against real data—its lighting, colors, sensor noise, annotations, and so on—to see how accurate they were. That was the first category. The second evaluated utility. Utility is whether, once the data is produced, it can ultimately serve the model effectively. Let me give an example. I think that going forward, data will increasingly be oriented toward utility. Utility is somewhat like the difference between buying an espresso and buying an iced coffee diluted with a lot of water. Right? Espresso greatly increases your level of alertness. I think future data will increasingly emphasize utility evaluation, raising the increment in information density and giving models more value from less and less data.

items.question: Why do you see synthetic data as valuable for addressing the edge cases Cruise’s driverless vehicles faced in San Francisco?
items.object: Synthetic data for Cruise’s driverless vehicles in San Francisco
items.answer: For instance, they wanted to launch their driverless vehicles first in San Francisco. Under those circumstances, the amount of data they could collect each day was relatively limited. How could they address edge-case scenarios? San Francisco has many homeless people, who may frequently dart in and out. It has many hills and slopes, and a great deal of fog. These are all difficult enough scenarios. They are not very common in the distribution, so the volume of data collected for them is not large. Yet these scenarios seriously affect driverless vehicles, especially their visual-perception algorithms. This creates a data problem: we need to solve small-sample events, but do not have enough data to train our models to solve such problems. On the other hand, we also want to discover more safety issues. But because we lack data, we cannot discover and validate similar safety issues either. By expanding real data with synthetic data, we could effectively discover more system-level safety issues. And in response to those issues, we could effectively solve them by expanding the data volume. It helped us achieve a faster iterative loop.

items.question: How do you use simulation and synthetic data to address rare incidents such as a pedestrian darting into the road?
items.object: Simulation and synthetic data for rare pedestrian road incidents
items.answer: Let’s take a pedestrian darting into the road. Data of this kind is relatively scarce. First, in simulation, starting from that scenario, we can create many kinds of pedestrians: different clothes, appearances, and body types—adults, children, elderly people—darting in and out in all sorts of ways. We can vary the surrounding scene: place them in the same lane or the opposite lane, alter the traffic conditions, and vary the weather and lighting to achieve diversity. We generalize a real problem we might encounter on the road into thousands or tens of thousands of problems. Using those scenarios, we can run our algorithms in simulation ten thousand times to see whether they encounter the same issues: whether the perception system fails, whether prediction fails, or whether the entire decision-making system can effectively avoid such problems. At the same time, once we find enough problems, we can feed the data—with its sufficiently accurate annotations—back into perception or prediction models, effectively improving those models. In that way, a small-sample event encountered on the road can help us solve as many more problems of that kind as possible.

items.question: How do you think the appropriate balance of synthetic and real data differs between autonomous driving and embodied intelligence?
items.object: The balance of synthetic and real data in autonomous driving and embodied intelligence
items.answer:
I do not think there is a fixed answer, because it depends. For a corner case or long-tail scenario, long-tail scenarios are so scarce that you may not encounter many in an entire year. Ideally, for every long-tail scenario, I might pair it with one thousand to ten thousand synthetic data samples. So the ratio is extremely high in that respect. But looking at the overall data picture, we also indeed use a lot of real data. Overall, at that time, roughly 30% of our data might have been synthetic. But for long-tail scenarios, we exceeded the 1-to-99 or 1-to-100 ratio Professor Wang He mentioned.

Of course, we are talking about autonomous driving. For embodied intelligence, it is quite different. Autonomous driving may keep synthetic data at 30% or less because the largest amount of data it needs is inevitably real: cars have existed for more than a century. Automakers such as Tesla, Li Auto, and Xiaomi have huge numbers of cars on the road, with good sensors and computing resources, constantly sending data back. Essentially, their costs are only computing and bandwidth. Drivers—the people who buy the cars—are effectively collecting that data for them, and that data volume is enormous. Therefore, for autonomous driving, especially today’s L2+ systems, the largest share of data is inevitably real. When they seek to improve a targeted problem, they may use far more synthetic data, especially for increasingly peripheral long-tail problems. But across the entire data mix, real data is inevitably the largest share.

For embodied intelligence, the situation is the opposite. Robots have not existed as a platform for a hundred years. We do not now have millions or tens of millions of real humanoid, dog-like, and other robots casually running around homes worldwide and generating data. Therefore, to truly advance embodied intelligence, we must first rely on massive amounts of synthetic data. And second, on a relatively small amount of real data; otherwise, the business model cannot work.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for a route centered on teleoperated real data to deploy embodied intelligence faster than a route centered on synthetic data?
items.object: Teleoperated real data as a path to deploying embodied intelligence
items.answer: A teleoperated robot would have to be sold and make money. How should I put it? I think that is difficult to imagine now. Let’s consider where such an opportunity might exist. One is OEMs. Domestic Chinese OEMs are already extremely automated. I do not think opportunities for humans to teleoperate robots, generate value, and make money are likely to appear in domestic OEMs. Among global OEMs, Germany, Japan, and the United States may have some such opportunities. But the problem is that teleoperation would first need to cross states or even countries, because labor costs remain high if it stays in the same state. Many U.S. states have restrictions prohibiting interstate teleoperation. So teleoperation is not that easy. And I think it is more likely only if you are an internal department within an OEM trying to optimize operations. If you are a company serving another OEM, it is also difficult because there are issues such as union politics. So Tesla may be the only possibility: using a real, potentially interstate teleoperation solution to improve efficiency in certain internal OEM processes. So I think Tesla could take that route. But for other companies of this kind, I think the overall likelihood is low. Consider hospitality, retail, and similar industries: the value created by teleoperating a robot versus its actual cost does not, in my view, produce such a high ROI. So, from an embodied-intelligence perspective overall, could a route centered on teleoperated real data iterate and deploy quickly—and be faster than a route centered on synthetic data? I do not think that is very likely.

items.question: What do you see as the hardest part of mapping the real world into simulation through Real2Sim?
items.object: Physical Real2Sim for robotics
items.answer: Let me first explain the underlying meaning of Real2Sim: it maps real scenarios, real assets, and the real world into simulation. Its requirement is not merely mapping visual reality into simulation; it is more about mapping physical reality into simulation. That is the hardest part, because many methods, including visual reconstruction, can solve the visual side. For the physical side, there are two foundational requirements. One is that the physics simulator must be good enough. The second is that every asset and scene you map must possess those physical properties. Take a simple example: a refrigerator has a pivot, hinges, and magnetic attraction. When you pull open its door, you may initially need considerable force; once it opens, as the pivot angle grows, the force you need becomes smaller. The refrigerator also has collision bodies. The door and drawers are each collision bodies that can collide with your hand, creating an interaction and force effect. For those hinges, collisions, and mechanical simulations, more physical parameters must be collected. For example, at different door angles, you need to collect how much force is needed to pull the refrigerator door open. Different refrigerator types vary. How do you collect the physical structure of the hinge? How do you set collision bodies? These are all parts of the physical reality-to-simulation process. For simulators, rigid-body simulators are relatively mature, but deformable bodies such as cloth remain more difficult. Fluids as well. Fundamentally, you must both bring back physical information and put it into simulation assets, and improve or build your underlying simulation engine. By combining those two, you can generate sufficiently accurate physical and mechanical information and ultimately obtain a correct output.

items.question: How do you evaluate whether a simulation is good?

items.answer: I think that is a key question. Our mission now is to make simulation successful. We can generally see that everyone is building simulation, and many papers and research topics study it. There are also increasingly many simulators trying to solve different problems. But very few people are truly focused on successful simulation, or the term “good simulation.” I think a good simulation must first support deployment: an algorithm trained in simulation must be able to be deployed. It may look like an object in my world, but the visual fidelity is inadequate, and it does not even have the most basic physical information. Even if some can open their doors, they may not comply with sufficiently correct physical information—such as having a sufficiently good hinge. Even if they have such information, the mechanics can be wrong: the weight is wrong, and the force required to pull open the door is wrong. Even if they have that, they do not have refrigerators sufficiently matching the distribution; perhaps they have only one single type of refrigerator.

Of course, good simulation also requires sufficiently accurate robots. A point people often overlook is that many robots, such as Unitree and others, have sufficiently good models in the real world, but their simulation models have many problems. We have encountered many customers whose problem is that a robot hand can lift one or two kilograms in the real world, but in simulation can lift only 0.1 kilograms. They have spent a long time tuning that hand—more than six months—and still have not tuned it well. So it is very different from what people imagine. On that basis, if we want to perform DeepSeek-like RL fine-tuning based on a large foundation model, we encounter another issue. items.question: What do you see as your core advantage in bringing real-world physical information into simulation through Real2Sim?
items.object: Physics-based Real2Sim and scalable production of simulation assets
items.answer: The first is Real2Sim: bringing physical information from the real world back and putting it into simulation. One aspect is accuracy; the second is scale efficiency. If retrieving the parameters of one refrigerator costs an extremely high amount, you cannot provide drinking-water-grade, high-quality simulation at scale. From our perspective, we have many underlying AI capabilities. These do not reconstruct based on vision, but based on physics. From information returned by key physical-data collection equipment and from information obtained through robot-object interactions, we can generate these core physical parameters relatively automatically. Then, through our complete toolchain and according to certain distributions, we generalize those parameters across different simulation assets and scenes. This is extremely critical. What I can say is that the basic raw materials used in simulation by the world’s best institutions are all produced by us. It is not that we are one of their simulation suppliers; we are their only simulation supplier—the only simulation supplier to the core institutions I just mentioned. This truly differentiates us from other key companies.

items.question: Why do you think of your Sim2Real platform as a playground for algorithm engineers?

items.answer: For Sim2Real, you can understand our positioning as essentially a playground. You should build a platform that lets anyone experiment quickly, and, once they find signals, scale quickly. At the foundation, this platform requires extensive assets and scenes, because they are raw materials: without them, there are no games for people to play in the playground. items.question: What do you think it takes to build full-stack simulation?
items.object: The capabilities required for full-stack simulation
items.answer: I think full-stack simulation is not just technology at its foundation; it combines four things. First is simulation technology. Second is engineering capability. Simulation is not purely an algorithmic or research project; it is more a set of large-scale engineering capabilities. So the second is engineering. Third is algorithms: for example, for Sim2Real and Real2Sim, you need algorithms that can retrieve these physical parameters. That creates a strong algorithmic requirement. But the fourth point is one most research companies do not want to touch: operations. This work cannot be separated from large-scale operations. Bringing back physical information from the world cannot be as simple as taking a photo and automatically getting the data. There must be humans in the loop. Second, testing the realism, effectiveness, and quality of simulation also cannot be completely automated, because people are the core standard for truly improving data quality. Look at Meta’s acquisition of Scale—it illustrates this point very well. Scale’s data keeps becoming more expensive. Why? Because the people it uses keep getting better. So data driven by people at the foundation is inevitably a core point.

items.question: How do you think synthetic-data companies should address the gap between synthetic and real data for robotics?
items.object: Addressing the gap between synthetic and real data for robotics
items.answer: I see it this way: from first principles, synthetic data will inevitably have problems, right? One is synthetic and one is real; there must be a gap, a shortfall. But I think the most important question is: at what magnitude of gap is the data still useful? That is the core question. Second, how can you continuously reduce that gap? Those are the two most important points. First, how do you know the magnitude of the gap? You need a complete synthetic-data capability; you must build full-stack algorithms and continually deploy robot algorithms. Only then can you understand where the gap is. If, as a synthetic-data company, you only handle data while your clients train the models, you can never know where the gap is, and you can never improve it. So the first point is having the ability to know the gap at any time. The second point is improving it through different means across the technology stack. For example, as I mentioned, in real-to-sim—going from reality to simulation—how can you enhance the diversity and accuracy of the information brought back from the real world? During simulation, how can you continually improve the underlying simulation engine? And in sim-to-real, how can you improve generalization and effectiveness? I think all of these are extremely important.

items.question: Why do you think specialization is necessary in the embodied-intelligence industry?
items.object: Specialization in the embodied-intelligence industry
items.answer: I think I can first explain it through a broad logic. I think embodied intelligence is extremely difficult. As we just mentioned, it involves simultaneously inventing a next-generation vehicle platform and inventing an L4 or even L5 algorithm for that vehicle. Essentially, it is inventing both things at once. Either one, I think, is harder than what Tesla is doing now in vehicles. Second, its algorithm began at L2, whereas the algorithms embodied intelligence needs are essentially L4 or L5. That makes the difficulty so high that specialization is necessary. It is unlikely that one company can both invent a platform and invent this algorithmic stack.

What they truly seek is to find the algorithm-and-data recipe for embodied intelligence—how to create a scaling-out recipe. That is what truly interests them. items.question: Why do you see synthetic data as important for scaling embodied intelligence?
items.object: Synthetic data for scaling embodied intelligence
items.answer: For example, how does PI collect data now? It rents all the apartments in San Francisco through Airbnb and has people collect data inside them. Think how much that costs. But fundamentally, those apartments are nowhere near enough. They have not thought much about scaling. To scale, they would need to rent more apartments and collect more data. The key thing about synthetic data is that it is the product of two things. Good data is the product of two things: first, diverse scenarios; second, high-quality human demonstrations. Large language models work the same way. Diverse, high-quality scenarios might include mathematics, computer science, programming, law, and medicine. Those are different scenarios. Human demonstrations initially might have people provide demonstrations for imitation learning. But now, for example, LLM data increasingly involves people setting a final exam question and letting the model repeatedly solve it with RL, to see whether it can achieve sufficiently good breakthroughs. It is a bit like a good teacher. An ordinary teacher gives demonstrations, but the best teacher sets questions, guiding students to improve continuously and tackle those problems. The same is true for embodied intelligence: diverse scenarios and high-quality human demonstrations. For scenarios, a core problem is rental cost. To collect hotel data, restaurant data, or home data, I need to rent or build those settings. Many teleoperation setups we see now have problems because they are mostly tabletop: apples, kettles, bottles, and so on are placed on a table, and a teleoperated arm collects data repeatedly. The scenarios are very single. They may build IKEA-like model rooms, but such setups have no generalization ability. To truly collect data through teleoperation, you must collect it in sufficiently realistic and diverse scenarios. That creates scenario-rental or scenario-construction costs. Autonomous driving does not have these problems. For synthetic data, you also have a scenario-building cost—you bring real physical data back and construct it—but its rental cost is very low. I can have one hundred or one thousand people in parallel, or use fully automated means, to generate data in those scenarios. That rental cost is essentially compute. This is synthetic data’s greatest advantage: the ability to efficiently scale up high-quality data across sufficiently distributed scenarios.

items.question: How do you explain the different opportunities and business models for AI companies in the United States and China?

They collect massive amounts of data, mainly through teleoperation, with many collection centers. After bringing back the data, they do imitation learning and finally perhaps a small amount of reinforcement learning for deployment. That is one category. Another is a simulation-centered route. items.question: How do you see Nvidia’s Isaac Sim and Google’s MuJoCo evolving as platforms for embodied simulation?
items.object: The convergence of Nvidia’s Isaac Sim and Google’s MuJoCo into an open-source embodied-simulation ecosystem
items.answer:
The world’s two best simulators may now be Isaac Sim and MuJoCo, and I think they will increasingly converge into one simulator. Simulation has four components: first, a physics solver—the physical simulation engine; second, rendering; third, sim-ready assets and scenes—assets and scenarios for embodied simulation; and fourth, APIs—the entire framework and toolchain. Isaac Sim uses PhysX for its underlying physics engine and Omniverse for rendering. Because of Omniverse, its industrial-grade simulation system, Nvidia has built an excellent rendering pipeline. Those are major advantages for Nvidia in embodied intelligence. MuJoCo’s core is the physics solver and the APIs above it. Its rendering has never been very good, because it has not invested in rendering as Nvidia has.

Why will they converge? PhysX, Isaac Sim’s underlying engine, has the key problem that it is somewhat old and poorly maintained. It was originally designed for games rather than embodied intelligence, so optimizing it for embodied intelligence takes a long time. Its code is also written in CUDA, which is difficult to understand and maintain. They will therefore use MuJoCo’s underlying physics solver and rewrite it using Nvidia’s GPU-accelerated language Warp, creating a new underlying physics engine called MuJoCo Warp. items.question: Why do you think a company working on simulation for embodied intelligence should build the simulator last?
items.object: Simulation and the priority of building a simulator
items.answer: I think people actually have a major misunderstanding about simulation. Whenever simulation comes up, people think of simulators and say, “Because simulators have certain problems, you therefore need to be a company that makes simulators in order to solve simulation.” But you will find that simulator companies have not been all that successful. Simulation is not the same thing as a simulator; a simulator is the physics engine I just mentioned. Simulation includes the simulator's physics engine, rendering, and scene ideas—that is, assets and scenes—as well as the downstream APIs and frameworks. The simulator is actually the innermost layer. Historically, simulators have often been closed-source, and their iteration cycles have been very slow, which makes it difficult for value to be transmitted down to the simulator layer. So there are relatively few people working on simulators, but they may give people a great deal of mystique. As a result, people think a simulation company must first build a simulator. But my core insight is that we will build the simulator last. Why? Because we believe the first reason simulation has not succeeded is that embodied intelligence has not had sufficiently high-quality assets and scenes. Next come frameworks and APIs, and only then the simulator. Of course, now that we have already built out the front end, we have many underlying simulator resources. But I think this is a relatively deep insight.

items.question: Why do you have such strong conviction in simulation as the key to bringing embodied intelligence into real-world deployment?
items.object: Simulation as a bet for real-world deployment of embodied intelligence
items.answer: The core bet is that simulation will definitely become the most crucial key factor in bringing embodied intelligence into real-world deployment. I think that when it comes to simulation, everyone has different understandings, or different beliefs. My belief is one of full conviction: I completely believe in it. Only with complete belief is it possible to truly drive its success. At the same time, because I completely believe in it, I think many things depend on human effort. Let me give an example. Before Musk began making electric vehicles, people might have said that no electric vehicle would succeed. At that point, Musk did not necessarily have more analytical information than everyone else; rather, he had a very strong belief in this matter, and he was also a core driving force in it, so he believed that things depend on human effort. If he had strong conviction and acted to make things happen, he could transform the reality as people understood it into another reality: electric vehicles would ultimately succeed. I believe I carry this conviction, and I believe I have the ability to truly let everyone ultimately receive the value of simulation.
